en: Abhidhānottara 4 = palm-leaf manuscript = Raghu Vīra’s manuscript reproduction by Lokesh Chandra
Then the Blessed One proclaimed the secret reality of the Vajraḍāka.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the successive sequence of names for the benefit of practitioners, clearly according to the lineage of gurus;
it is free from external conceptual construction and is the supreme commitment of equanimity.
Free from doubt, free from conventional conduct, and devoid of all fear.
Neither the lunar day nor the asterism is prescribed, nor is fasting enjoined;
whether one is pure or impure, neither ritual purity nor water-libations are required.
Free from the constraints of specific times, having abandoned the rules of ritual purity and conventional conduct,
he is one who knows the independent application of mantras and is devoted solely to the welfare of all sentient beings.

In mountain caves and groves, on riverbanks and at confluences, on the delightful shores of the great ocean, under a solitary tree, in a temple of Śiva, in a mother-house, or in a cremation ground, or in various excellent gardens.
In a monastery, in a shrine, in a cave, or in a house, or at a crossroads.

The practitioner should accomplish the yoga that bestows the fruit of all desires. Having prepared a designated place, or wherever the mind finds delight, there the perfection of the practice is achieved; this is considered the manifold vow (*saṃvara*).
Meditation is performed through many varieties according to the dispositions of those to be trained;
one should perform the smearing of the ground with the nectar of the five wisdoms.
One should diligently offer a profusion of flowers of the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā),
being well-composed upon a beautiful seat marked with the Viśvamudrā,
while focusing on the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) with a one-pointed mind.
Practice the four means of attraction through the four divine abodes;
taking the ten wholesome paths as your object, bring about the welfare and prosperity of all sentient beings.
One should perceive the emptiness of all phenomena, both external and internal;
indeed, one should abide in mind-only, which is the supreme equipment for awakening.
One should meditate on a moon mandala situated in the center of the lotus within the heart-sphere;
having seen that, which is the supreme reality, auspicious, and composed of the five gnoses.

Having exhorted the previously accomplished ones (*pūrvasiddha*), one should cause them to perform the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of this divine [mandala], which consists of various rays of light and flashes forth on all sides.
Having seen the supreme maṇḍala in the delightful abode of the element of space,
and having seen the wrathful goddesses all around like sesame seeds in a heap;
Having seen the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, the bodhicitta, the Guru, and the Lord, the Goddess, consisting of worship itself, should perform the ninefold worship.
The Yoginī should emanate floods of Buddhas and Wrathful Kings;
she should establish all sentient beings of the six realms in the state of Buddhahood.
Having seen them, they all enter right there into the midst of those called the space-realm (khadhātu),
and they go for refuge to the Three Jewels until they reach the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
There, all sentient beings should be established in the state of enlightenment;
having requested the practitioners there, they should constantly go for refuge.
One should generate the virtuous mind of ego-identity regarding the five aggregates and so forth:
form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— [visualized as] *bhrūṃ āḥ hrīḥ hoḥ hūṃ*.
Vairocana, Vajrasūrya, and likewise Padmanarteśvara;
he who is known as Vajrarāja, and another, Vajrasattva;
in the state of all Tathāgatas, Śrī Herukavajra—Hrīḥ.
The eye, the ear, the nose, the mouth, the body, and likewise the mind;
Oṃ Hūṃ Trāṃ Āḥ Khaṃ Haṃ;
delusion, hatred, as well as envy, passion, and even avarice.
The Vajra of Sovereignty over all sense-bases (*āyatana*) consists of earth,
water, fire, wind, and space,
[expressed as] *lāṃ*, *māṃ*, *pāṃ*, *tāṃ*, and *khaṃ*.
The goddess Padmajvālinī is the one who casts down, the one who slays, the one who attracts, and the one who causes to dance; she is equal to space and like the sky.
Thus, the yogi dwells within the ordinary aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
"All phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature. Thus one should effect purification.
Thereafter, one should go for the three refuges; one will become the embodiment of the mantra.
Having become Heruka myself for the sake of the benefit of all sentient beings, I shall then establish them all in the state of Heruka, the unsurpassed state.

"Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature"—one should recite this three times. One should establish a mass of light reaching from the base up to the peak of existence throughout the ten directions.
Then, having seen that mass of light, one likewise sees a rampart and a cage.
One should establish the vajra-ground and the canopy above, as well as the two nets of arrows;
one should place the blazing wall of vajra-fire far outside of that.
Oṃ, O Earth, become vajra; vajra-binding, hūṃ!
Oṃ vajraprākāra hūṃ vaṃ hūṃ.
Oṃ vajrapañjara hūṃ paṃ hūṃ.
Oṃ vajravitāna hūṃ khaṃ hūṃ.
Oṃ vajra-arrow-net trāṃ śaṃ trāṃ.
Oṃ vajrajvālānalārka hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ.
Then, having seen the brilliantly radiant eight-spoked wheel of Heruka’s gnosis situated in the center of a solar mandala, one should visualize Vajrasattva.

Three-faced and six-armed, peaceful, with the brilliant luster of pure crystal and the moon; resplendent with the Mahāmudrā, absorbed in the Mahāmudrā; well-established in the posture of wisdom (prajñāparyaṅka). [3]
Wearing a crown of a garland of skulls with Akṣobhya as its crest-jewel,
fully adorned with all ornaments, marked with all the primary characteristics,
and embellished with the secondary marks.
Holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga, embraced by a bell and a vajra,
the hero holds a noose and a goad, abiding in the state of great bliss.
White, yellow, and green, with distorted faces on both sides;
then one should expand the eightfold wrathful deities in both forward and reverse order.
One should install these wrathful deities: Vajracaṇḍānalārka, Vajroṣṇīṣa, Kuṇḍalī, Vajrayakṣa, the mighty Vajrakāla, and the one named Vajrabhiṣaja.
Blue, yellow, red, green, smoky-grey,
white, black, and dark-red— these terrifying beings, formidable with their bared fangs.
She has three faces and six arms, all resplendent with ornaments of human bone;
she sits in the ālīḍha posture in the center of a sun disc upon a double lotus.
One should contemplate the eight world-protectors as being trampled underfoot;
[the principal deity] holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, while the others hold nooses and goads,
and all carry bells and ḍamaru drums.
Facing her who is embraced by Prajñā, with tawny hair standing on end and distorted,
terrifying with prominent fangs, and wearing a tiger-skin garment—
one should visualize oneself as Vajrahūṃkāra, turned toward her.
Fierce, filled with the flames of anger, and terrifyingly formidable and awe-inspiring.
Adorned with all ornaments, standing firm in the ālīḍha posture,
he holds a goad, a noose, and a khaṭvāṅga staff, along with a bell, a vajra, and a skull-cup.

One should meditate upon Vajrabhairava in the crown of Vajrasattva, whose body is adorned with a garland of severed heads, who bears a fierce crest of skulls, who tramples upon all the wicked, and who is endowed with wisdom.
Then one should contemplate the upward movement and visualize two wrathful deities.
Upon the *uṣṇīṣa* is a vajra-skull-cup with the luster of cool, dark blue collyrium,
holding a skull-bowl and a *khaṭvāṅga*, as well as a vajra-spear and a skull-cup.
Holding a noose, a goad, a vajra, and a bell, he stands in the ālīḍha posture.
The wrathful deities of the *kīla* should radiate forth there into the ten directions;
having given the command right there, the Guru renders them free from obstacles.
Having thus recollected that name, one should join the index finger with the thumb and snap the fingers toward the four directions and the ten directions.
Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha hūṃ phaṭ || [To] the East.
Oṃ gṛhṇa 2 hūṃ phaṭ || [Direction: North.
Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya 2 hūṃ phaṭ || [In the] western [direction].
Oṃ ānaya hoḥ, O Blessed One, King of Vidyās, hūṃ phaṭ! [In the south.]
And with this king of mantras, one should plant the eightfold stake for all obstacles, both in direct and reverse order.

Oṃ gha gha ghātaya ghātaya sarvavighnān hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ kīlaya kīlaya sarvapāpān hūṃ phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! Vajrakīlaya, the Holder of the Vajra, commands: pierce the vajras of the body, speech, and mind of all wicked obstructing hosts! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Strike with the vajra-kila by gazing with the wrathful eye;
having struck in both forward and reverse order, O Vajra, accomplish it—dhīḥ!
Oṃ vajra hūṃ mudgara vajrakīlākoṭaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Thereafter, one possessing the wisdom of Krodhavajra should recite this mantra:
Oṃ kha vajradhṛk vajrahūṃkāra vajra hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ vajracaṇḍa vajra hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ vajranalārka vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ vajroṣṇīṣa vajra hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ vajrakuṇḍali vajra hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ vajrayakṣa vajra hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ vajrakāla vajra hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ vajramahābala vajra hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ vajra hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ Vajrabhīṣaṇa vajra hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ vajra-uṣṇīṣa-cakravarti hūṃ phaṭ | [6] Oṃ vajra-pātāla vajra hūṃ phaṭ ||
In this way, the command indeed succeeds, and the forest of obstacles is destroyed in an instant;
[those] who consume meat, marrow, and fat, provided with white and red [substances], [attain success].
The yogi should roll the pill and consume it; he will certainly attain accomplishment.
Blue and yellow, with the vajra-hūṃkāra in the center;
yellow and black, green, and smoke-colored-yellow.
Green, white, and yellow, and green; red-yellow, and green;
for others as well, it is according to their respective crowns.
Holding the three vajras, they rejoice in you, who are the unshakable commitment.
For this is the samaya of all wrathful ones, the crusher of misfortune;
thus the Leader assumes various such commands of many kinds.
Having seen the one who is free from obstacles and full of compassion, where the yogis abide—
whether he be naked or not naked, with ashes on his limbs and hair loose— whoever [sees him thus]...
In this way, one should meditate upon and recite the wheel so that the desired result arises;
and while focused on the consumption [of offerings], one should remember the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
Oṃ āḥ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of signs.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of the wishless.
One should conceptualize mere appearance, mere consciousness, and mere mental consciousness as being "mind-only.
These phenomena are like one's own reflection; they are neither phenomena nor the nature of phenomena.
Like space, it is untainted, devoid of intrinsic nature, and untroubled;
for when the fire is burning within the hollow of the right hand, the activity of the mind flows forth as if it were subtle vision. [6]
The entire triple world clearly enters into non-duality; I bow to that Dharmadhātu, the light of the sun. O yogin who has reached the end, you move with all your senses.
And when ignorance has been completely destroyed by the presence of all the Victors, the triple world attains the state of being the cause of tranquility;
for him, the glorious *ālaya* becomes as unobstructed as space.
Through the yoga of the recollection of the Buddha, one cultivates the recollection of the Dharma;
through the yoga of the recollection of the Dharma, one becomes the Dharmakāya oneself.
For those who know the supreme reality, there is no doubt that they will produce this [state] from the midst of the intellect through the constant practice of its manifestation.
The single, imperishable bindu indeed dwells eternally in the heart.
For those men who cultivate that through the yoga of recollecting supreme beings (*parasattva*) and the yoga of recollecting beings (*sattva*), knowledge arises; this is cultivation.
One should contemplate the sentient being through the dharma of the recollection of sentient beings.
Having seen the power of his vow, and seeing that he is compassionate in nature for the sake of others' welfare,
one should contemplate the circle of wind as far as the elixir (rasāyana).
One should meditate on that which is born from the syllable YAṂ, resembling a bow, produced from the color blue,
marked with a banner, moving, and filled with a dense mass of smoke-colored garlands.
Above that, one should meditate on a triangular mandala of fire, red in color, filled with garlands of flames, marked with vajras, and produced from the syllable RAṂ.
Like another ten million suns.
Above that, one should meditate upon the supreme Vāruṇa [mandala], born from the syllable *vaṃ*,
resembling snow, circular, and garlanded with rays; above that, one should meditate upon the yellow [mandala] born from the syllable *laṃ*.
A square, marked with a vajra-array and intensely filled with yellow rays—
upon that, the yogi should visualize Sumeru, the supreme of mountains, square,
composed of the four jewels, and adorned with eight peaks.
Born from the syllable *suṃ*, it is delightful, possessing the most excellent and supreme divine splendor.

In that very place, one should visualize a peaked pavilion situated behind [the central deity], containing the eternal Śāśvata born from the syllable *Bhṛṃ*, with its excellent wheel turned toward him.
It is square, with four gates adorned by four archways;
it is marked with necklaces and half-necklaces, and beautified with silk ribbons and flower garlands.
In all the corner sections and at the junctions of the gates and projections,
one should mark out the outer maṇḍala, inlaid with vajra-jewels.
Inside that is an eight-spoked wheel of white color.
In its center is a great lotus of variegated colors with eight petals, fully blossomed, its pericarp and filaments crowded with a natural garland.
In the center of the lunar mandala, however, is Vajrasattva, born together with his consort.
White, yellow, red, and green, with four faces;
the peaceful face is green, while the wrathful face is distorted, fierce, and terrifying.
She is in union with Vajraghaṇṭa and holds a trident, an axe, and a ḍamaru drum;
she carries a curved knife, a skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and is draped in the skin of Brahmā.
Likewise, with twelve arms he holds a noose and the Brahmaśiras [missile];
seated upon a corpse in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, he is resplendent with a crown of skulls.
Complete with all ornaments and endowed with the primary and secondary marks,
he has the Wisdom-Samaya in his heart and the Vajra-holder upon his crown.
Just as there is skillful means, so too is wisdom; having distinguished the five supreme Vajradhātveśvarīs according to their respective families, they are empowered by the five mudrās.

Through the yoga of the means of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the two bodies are liquefied; immediately upon arising, Kāyadaṅkā together with his retinue and the heroines (*vīrayoginī*) stands in the *ālīḍha* and *pratyālīḍha* postures, with faces that are white, yellow, red, and green.
In the arms engaged in the embrace of the Vajra-bell, according to the previous sequence beginning with Vajrasattva,
he holds the hand-symbols and a garland of skulls, adorned with a necklace of fifty severed heads.
He wears a crescent moon, has a face made terrifying by protruding fangs,
possesses three eyes and twelve arms, treads upon the gods of the Brahma-realm, is adorned with ornaments of human bone, and bears a crown of Vairocana.
Adorned with the six mudrās and wearing a tiger-skin garment,
her body is embraced from the front by the Buddha-Ḍākinī; she holds a skull-cup in embrace and possesses a vajra for threatening the wicked.

Embracing him with her two arms, she was overwhelmed by the longing for sexual union. She struck the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*) situated within the aggregates, bases, and elements, causing it to fall. [4]
The water element shall not kill me.
The fire element is the attractor of the earth.
The wind element is that Narteśvarī.
The space element is Kha-Padmajālinī.
Yellow, blue, golden, fair, red, smoke-colored, and dark blue.
In the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is Vairocana, Oṃ, white in color;
in sensation (vedanā) is Ratnavajra, Āṃ, the color of molten gold; in perception (saṃjñā) is Padmanarteśvara, Hrīḥ, red.
The formation aggregate is Vajrarāja, green in color, with the syllable *hoḥ*.
Within consciousness is Vajrasattva, white in color, with the syllable *hūṃ*.
In the state of all Tathāgatas is Śrī Heruka, black in color, with the syllable *hrīḥ*.
In the two eyes is white Mohavajra;
in the two ears are two black Dveṣavajras marked with HŪṂ;
in the nose is yellow Īrṣyāvajra marked with KHAṂ.
In the mouth is Rāgavajra, syllable ĀḤ, red in color;
in touch is Mātsaryavajra, syllable HŪṂ, green in color;
in all the sense bases is Aiśvaryavajra, syllable HAṂ, white.
In the body, HŪṂ is white;
in speech, ĀḤ is red in color;
in the mind, OṂ is black in color.
In this way, one should preside over the objects of body, speech, and mind from the center.
There, on the eastern petal is Ḍākinī, blue in color;
on the northern petal is Lāmā, green in color;
and on the western [petal] is Khaṇḍarohā, red in color.
To the south is Rūpiṇī, golden-yellow in color.
She has one face, four arms, and three eyes; her hair is disheveled and she wears no clothes.
Supreme, she stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, formidable, fierce, and terrifying, adorned with the five mudrās.
Her hands hold a skull-cup (*kapāla*), a khaṭvāṅga staff, a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), and a curved knife (*kartti*).
Hoḥ! They cause passion in the mouth by gazing with a passionate look.
Furthermore, in the intermediate directions, there are four skull-cups of bodhicitta upon four jars of the five nectars.
On the eastern spoke of the body wheel, in Pretapuri, is Mahābalacakravega, who is black.
In the north, at the house-deity, is yellow Ratnavajra Khaṇḍarohā.
In the west, in Saurāṣṭra, there is Hayagrīvaśauṇḍinī, who is red.
In the south, on Suvarṇadvīpa, there is Ākāśagarbha-cakravarmiṇī, who is green.
In the city of the southeast is Śrī Herukasuvīrā, who is red.
In the southwest, at Sindhū, Padmanarteśvara and Mahābalā are white as the moon.
In the northwest, in Maru, is Vairocanacakravartinī, greyish-smoky in color.
In the northeast, at Kulatā, the great hero Vajrasattva is white.
The heroes, Mahābala and the others, have one face and four arms;
they wear crests of matted hair and turbans, and their two embracing arms hold a wheel and a bell,
while the other two arms hold a khaṭvāṅga staff and a ḍamaru drum.
They stand with their bodies adorned with the five mudrās and in the ālīḍha posture.
The goddesses, beginning with Cakravegā, likewise have one face and two arms; they embrace [the central deity], hold skull-cups in their hands, and brandish wheels while threatening the wicked.
Three-eyed, of fierce form, adorned with loose, flowing hair,
absorbed in non-dual yoga, supreme, and clad in the directions as their garments;
[they possess] necklaces, crest-jewels, armlets, earrings, and sacred threads.
With a garland of skulls adorning his neck, he was accompanied by the jingling sounds of his girdle and anklets.

At the eastern, northern, western, and southern gates are Kākāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, Śvānāsyā, and Sūkarāsyā; in the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast are Yamadāḍhī, Yamadūtī, Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī, and Yamamathanī.

Just as it is for the host of ḍākinīs, so it is for Kākāsyā and the others according to their distinctions; likewise, the goddesses situated in the intermediate directions possess two beautiful forms,
seated upon corpses, most terrible, and striving for the sake of all beings through compassion.
Upon the foreheads of all these heroes is a garland of wheels.

Thus, in the body wheel, the inhabitants of the netherworld praise the Blessed One, their faces turned toward the various aesthetic sentiments through the casting of diverse and manifold glances and gestures by the heroes and yoginīs of the maṇḍala.
Having attained [the state], the Great Bliss (Mahāsukha) egg of passion sleeps; *alalala hoḥ*!
By this song being sung, the emanations of internal existence—[the Great Bliss, the entirety of the Tathāgatas, and the intended object]—are produced.
The Tathāgatas, who are utterly pure, indeed fashion the maṇḍala. Some yogins desire it to be like the cool current of a womb-born being.
One should draw in the body-wheel, which is womb-born, by means of the maṇḍala of gnosis, and cause it to enter through worship and praise.
Through the yoga of emanation and reabsorption, the yogi who contemplates existence and non-existence as a bed conquers; by the performance of ten thousand blue dyes,
he accomplishes a womb-born body and the state of moving through space— of this there is no doubt.
Oṃ śrīkāyadaṅka rurulu bhrūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ḍākinījālasamvara svāhā. [Heart mantra]
Oṃ bhrūṃ haṃ haṃ bhrūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the *upahṛdaya* (near-heart mantra).
Oṃ buddhaḍākinye bhrūṃ vairocanīye hūṃ phaṭ. [This is] the heart mantra.
Oṃ bhrūṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye hūṃ bhrūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the upahr̥daya (near-heart mantra).
Oṃ kṣmāṃ Mahābala kṣmāṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ || [5] Oṃ Cakravege hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ||
Oṃ hāṃ ratnavajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ khaṇḍarohe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ hrīḥ Hayagrīva hrīḥ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ sauṇḍinīye hūṃ 2 phaṭ || [6] Oṃ hūṃ ākāśagarbha hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ||
Oṃ cakravarmiṇīye hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ kili śrīheruka kili hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ, O heroic one, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ siliya narteśvara sili hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ Mahābale hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ hrīṃ vairocana hili hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ cakravartinīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ dhiri vajrasattva dhiri hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ, O you of great heroism, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ Kākāsyā hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ ulukāsye hūṃ 2 phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the dog-faced one, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, O sow-faced one, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ yamadāḍhi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ yamadūti hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ yamadaṃṣṭriṇi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ Yamamathani hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ ḍākinīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ rāme hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ khaṇḍarohe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ rūpiṇīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Thus, one should worship the names of the Ḍākinīs and others at the beginning upon the lotuses.
Accomplishment always arises from that which consists of fivefold nature; it is not otherwise. Likewise, there are pacification, subjugation, delusion, and immobilization.
That which is to be performed by Kāyaḍāka brings about eternal accomplishment (*siddhi*).
[5] At the time of rising, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*); then the heroic yoginīs will be seen through the radiance of pure gnosis.
Oṃ bhrūṃ at the heart; Namaḥ āṃ at the head.
Svāhā! Ho! On the head.
Vauṣaṭ Hei: the armor.
Bhrūṃ Hūṃ Ho: the two eyes.
Phaṭ Haḥ: the weapon.
One should visualize [them] with six colors: white, yellow, red, blue, green, and smoky-grey.
Oṃ haḥ ā at the navel: Buddhaḍākinī;
ho hūṃ at the heart: Yāminī.
Aṃ mau: the face is the enchanting one.
Oṃ hreṃ hrīṃ, to Saṃcālanī at the head.
HO HŪṂ, Saṃtrāsanī at the crest-lock, PHAṬ!
NAMAḤ Caṇḍikā, the weapon for all limbs!
"One dwells in the *kāyadaṇḍakas* of all heroes and yoginīs"—
thus, in the yoga with one's own tutelary deity, one should conceptualize everything in this way.
One should consume the nectar of the five wisdoms and dwell at ease;
with the Vajra of the Pledge of Worship, one should practice during the four junctions of the day.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Chapter on the Method for Restraint of the Body.
